items.text: Remote work wasn't a privilege for neurodivergent people — it was the accommodation nobody had to formally request. RTO is quietly taking that away, and most people don't know they may have legal grounds to push back.
items.rationale: Anchors the RTO angle in a reframe that lands immediately and is defensible from the sources. Ends on actionable orientation without giving legal advice.
items.sensitivity_flag: 'Legal grounds' is directional, not prescriptive, and accurately reflects disability accommodation law — but could read as legal advice. The intent is to flag the option exists, not to advise on a specific case. Acceptable as written; monitor replies for misreads.

items.text: 81% of Fortune 500 companies now have live RTO policies. HR teams are reporting a spike in neurodiversity accommodation requests because of it. If going back is wrecking you, that's a workplace rights question — not a personal failure.
items.rationale: Uses the concrete stat to ground urgency in current reality, then pivots to human stakes. Reframes 'struggling' as potentially legitimate rather than weak without overclaiming.
items.sensitivity_flag: Verify the 81% figure directly from the Allwork.space source before posting — the briefing cites it but the primary source should be confirmed.

items.text: Burnout isn't the absence of effort. It's proof you spent more than a nervous system can maintain. For autistic people, that tab includes masking, sensory load, and social processing — none of which anyone else sees on the ledger.
items.rationale: Directly counters the 'lazy' narrative with a grounded, unsentimental frame. The ledger metaphor earns its place without requiring clinical vocabulary.

items.text: Fine all day. Falls apart at home. That's not weakness or performance. That's a nervous system that rationed everything it had to keep you upright — and has nothing left by evening.
items.rationale: Names the end-of-day collapse pattern directly and without jargon. Short, punchy, recognition-first — will hit readers who have felt this without ever seeing it named.

items.text: For PDAers, 'I should shower' can hit the same way as 'your boss needs this now.' The avoidance isn't stubbornness. It's a nervous system treating any demand — internal or external — as a threat.
items.rationale: Names the internal-demand piece of PDA — the most undersaturated and widely misunderstood dimension — with a concrete, relatable example rather than abstract language.

items.text: The PDA piece most people miss: it comes for things you actually want to do. The moment something becomes 'I ought to' — even if you chose it — it can become undoable. That confusion is real. It's not a character flaw.
items.rationale: Targets the internal-demand paradox with a micro-insight frame. The final sentence is the validation payoff that counters shame without being preachy.

items.text: The grief after a late autism diagnosis isn't grief for being autistic. It's grief for every year spent not knowing. The misdiagnoses. The friendships. The accommodations that never came.
items.rationale: Precisely names the relief-and-grief paradox documented in the 2026 PubMed study. The list structure lets the weight land without over-explaining.
items.sensitivity_flag: The list of losses could read as universal rather than a widely documented pattern; the PubMed source and the lived-experience writing in the briefing back this up as common, but 'for many' could be added before the list items if the team prefers explicit hedging.

items.text: Unmasking isn't taking off a mask you've been wearing. It's building a face you were never given the chance to grow. Research is finally naming what the community has long known: reclamation, not removal.
items.rationale: The Frontiers in Psychiatry paper is the news peg. The reframe is accurate to the research and more hopeful than 'stop hiding' — will resonate with anyone in early or mid identity-work.

items.text: AuDHD, briefly: crave routine and novelty. Need people and get flattened by them. Want structure and can't build it. Neither the ADHD nor the autistic playbook covers all of this. Both fit half.
items.rationale: Compresses the 'internal civil war' angle into a punchy recognition-first list. Closes with the 'half-right in every space' observation that makes AuDHD people feel seen without pathologizing the experience.

items.text: What's your AuDHD opposite pull — the one that makes every piece of advice feel like it was written for someone slightly different from you?
items.rationale: Lean discussion-opener that invites personal responses without manufacturing drama. The phrasing respects individual variation rather than implying a universal AuDHD experience.

items.text: PDA: Pathological Demand Avoidance or Persistent Drive for Autonomy. The name isn't settled — and that's not an accident. One encodes a deficit seen from the outside. One encodes a need felt from within. Which do you use, and why?
items.rationale: Raises the naming debate honestly without declaring a winner. 'Encodes a deficit' vs 'encodes a need' crystallizes what the fight is actually about, inviting informed community response.

items.text: Low-demand parenting isn't removing all limits. It's being honest about which ones are worth the nervous-system cost — and discovering most of them aren't.
items.rationale: Addresses the 'permissiveness' criticism head-on with a tight reframe. 'Discovering most of them aren't' is the disarming payload — a quiet challenge to convention-driven demands without lecturing parents.
